chunks: And from him from Safwan from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who died and had no wealth and had not performed the Hajj of Islam, so some of his brothers performed Hajj on his behalf. He said (peace be upon him): 'Does that suffice for him or is it deficient?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Rather, it is a complete Hajj.'
If a man bequeaths a Hajj, and if it is the Hajj of Islam, it is taken from all his wealth as we mentioned earlier, and if it is a voluntary Hajj, it is taken from one-third of his wealth. Narrated.

key_terms.حَجَّةَ الْإِسْلَامِ: The obligatory Hajj performed once in a lifetime
key_terms.حَسَبَ مَا قَدَّمْنَاهُ: As previously mentioned (referring to prior context in the chapter)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a deceased person's obligatory Hajj if they died without wealth, and who pays for it?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudence of Hajj for the deceased, affirming that a proxy’s performance suffices as a complete discharge of the obligatory duty even if the deceased lacked personal wealth. It further distinguishes the financial burden by stipulating that the cost of the obligatory Hajj is deducted from the entire estate, whereas a voluntary (Nafl) Hajj is paid from one-third of the estate, reflecting the principle of voluntary bequests in Shia inheritance law.
